sections.title: 1. Critical Resources & The `counter++` Race Condition
sections.description: How machine-level load/add/store interleaving causes lost updates—and why N = 1,000,000 can yield a minimum of 2.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a Lost Update (`counter = counter + 1`)
blocks.content:
A **critical resource** (*ressource critique*) is a non-shareable resource accessed by multiple tasks—either a logical resource (e.g., a global variable read and written by multiple threads) or a physical resource (e.g., a peripheral). The portion of code accessing it is a **critical section** (*section critique*), bracketed by an **entry protocol** (*prélude*) and an **exit protocol** (*postlude*).

When two threads each run `counter = counter + 1` $N = 1\,000\,000$ times, the single C++ statement compiles to three non-atomic machine instructions:

```asm
mov counter, r1   ; 1. Load shared counter into private register r1
addi 1, r1        ; 2. Increment local register r1
mov r1, counter   ; 3. Store r1 back to shared counter
```

### Slide 7 Trace: A Single Lost Update (`counter = 10`)

Suppose `counter = 10` initially and both tasks execute one increment:

1. **T1** executes `mov counter, r1` $\rightarrow$ `T1.r1 = 10`.
2. **Context switch** to T2 before T1 increments or writes back.
3. **T2** executes all three instructions: `r1 <- 10`, `r1 <- r1 + 1` (`11`), `counter <- r1` (**`counter` becomes `11`**).
4. **Context switch** back to T1.
5. **T1** resumes with its stale `T1.r1 = 10`: `r1 <- r1 + 1` (`11`), `counter <- r1` (**`counter` is overwritten with `11`**).

Result: **`counter` is `11` instead of `12`**—one update was completely lost.

blocks.title: Classic Exam Proof: Why the Theoretical Minimum for N = 1,000,000 is `2`
blocks.content:
With 2 threads each looping $N = 1\,000\,000$ times, what is the **theoretical minimum** final value of `counter`? **Answer: `2`** (not `1,000,000` and not `1`!).

| Step | T1 (`r1`) | `counter` (Shared) | T2 (`r1`) | What Happens |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **0 (Init)** | — | `0` | — | Initial state before either thread starts |
| **1** | `0` | `0` | — | **T1** starts iteration 1: `mov counter, r1` (`r1 = 0`), then gets **preempted** |
| **2** | `0` | `999,999` | `999,999` | **T2** runs `999,999` full iterations (1 iteration left!) |
| **3** | `1` | `1` | `999,999` | **T1** resumes iteration 1: `addi 1, r1` (`1`), `mov r1, counter` (**wipes out 999,999!**) |
| **4** | `1` | `1` | `1` | **T2** starts its final iteration (`1,000,000`th): `mov counter, r1` (`r1 = 1`), then gets **preempted** |
| **5** | `1,000,000` | `1,000,000` | `1` | **T1** completes its remaining `999,999` iterations (`counter` reaches `1,000,000`) and exits |
| **6** | `1,000,000` | **`2`** | `2` | **T2** resumes its final iteration: `addi 1, r1` (`2`), `mov r1, counter` (**writes `2`!**) |

> [!TIP]
> **Why is `1` impossible?** To end at `counter = 1`, the *very last* store in the entire execution must write `1`, meaning that thread loaded `0` on its **final** iteration. For $N > 1$, if a thread loads `0` on iteration 1 and gets preempted, it still has $N - 1$ iterations left after writing `1`—so it cannot both wipe out the other thread's work *and* have its very first write be the final write of the program. Thus the minimum for $N \ge 2$ is always **`2`**.

blocks.title: The 4 Rules of Mutual Exclusion & Slide 16 Fairness Types
blocks.content:
Every valid mutual exclusion algorithm must satisfy **4 rules** (Slide 17):

1. **Mutual Exclusion (*Exclusion mutuelle*):** At any instant, at most **one** task may be in the critical section.
2. **No Deadlock (*Absence d'interblocage / Liveness*):** If several tasks are waiting to enter the critical section while no task is inside, one of them must be able to enter in finite time.
3. **Independence (*Pas de couplage*):** The behavior of a task *outside* the critical section and its entry/exit protocols must have **no influence** on the mutual exclusion algorithm (e.g., crashing or stopping in the non-critical section must never block other tasks).
4. **Symmetry (*Symétrie*):** No task plays a privileged role; the solution is identical for all tasks.

### Starvation (*Famine*) & Waiting Fairness Types (Slide 16)

Beyond avoiding deadlock, an algorithm must avoid **starvation** (*famine*), where a task is perpetually bypassed by others. When multiple tasks request a critical resource, the entry protocol's waiting fairness can be classified into **4 types**:

| Fairness Type | Definition (Slide 16) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **FIFO** | Tasks enter strictly in the order they requested the resource (First-In, First-Out). |
| **Linéaire** (*Linear*) | A task **cannot** access the resource **twice** if another task is currently waiting (at most 1 bypass). |
| **Bornée par $f(n)$** (*Bounded by $f(n)$*) | For $n$ tasks, a waiting task cannot be overtaken by more than $f(n)$ other tasks. |
| **Finie** (*Finite*) | The wait is **not bounded** by a function of $n$, **but not infinite** (guaranteed eventual entry). |

sections.title: 2. Why Naive Attempts Fail (Attempts 1–5)
sections.description: Full C++ implementations and step-by-step failure traces for all 5 naive attempts from Slides 20–24.

blocks.title: Attempt 1 (Slide 20): Shared `bool occupe` — Fails: No Mutual Exclusion

annotations.note: Test and set are separate instructions! A preemption between line 5 and line 7 breaks exclusion.

blocks.title: Attempt 1 Failure Trace
blocks.content:
**Failure Mode:** **Pas d'exclusion** (No Mutual Exclusion).
1. `occupe` is `false`.
2. `T0` evaluates `while (occupe)` $\rightarrow$ `false`, exits loop, and is **preempted** before `occupe = true`.
3. `T1` evaluates `while (occupe)` $\rightarrow$ still `false`! `T1` sets `occupe = true` and enters the **critical section**.
4. `T0` resumes, sets `occupe = true`, and **also enters the critical section**.

blocks.title: Attempt 2 (Slide 21): Strict Turn `int tour` — Fails: Coupling

annotations.note: If T0 stops or sleeps in its non-critical section when tour == 0, T1 is blocked forever!

blocks.title: Attempt 2 Failure Trace
blocks.content:
**Failure Mode:** **Couplage** (Strict Alternation — violates Rule 3: Independence).
1. `tour` starts at `0`. `T0` enters and exits the critical section, setting `tour = 1`.
2. `T0` then **stops** (or runs very slowly) in its **non-critical section**.
3. `T1` enters and exits the critical section, setting `tour = 0`.
4. `T1` wants to enter the critical section a second time, but `tour == 0`—and `T0` will never set `tour = 1` because `T0` is in its non-critical section. **`T1` is blocked forever** even though the CS is free.

blocks.title: Attempt 3 (Slide 22): `bool etat[2]` Check-Then-Set — Fails: No Mutual Exclusion

annotations.note: Checking the other's flag before raising your own has the exact same race window as Attempt 1.

blocks.title: Attempt 3 Failure Trace
blocks.content:
**Failure Mode:** **Pas d'exclusion** (No Mutual Exclusion).
1. `etat = {false, false}`.
2. `T0` checks `while (etat[1])` $\rightarrow$ `false`, and is **preempted** before `etat[0] = true`.
3. `T1` checks `while (etat[0])` $\rightarrow$ still `false`! `T1` sets `etat[1] = true` and enters the **critical section**.
4. `T0` resumes, sets `etat[0] = true`, and **also enters the critical section**.

blocks.title: Attempt 4 (Slide 23): `bool etat[2]` Set-Then-Check — Fails: Deadlock

annotations.note: Setting etat[0] = true first guarantees mutual exclusion, but if both set their flags simultaneously, both spin forever.

blocks.title: Attempt 4 Failure Trace
blocks.content:
**Failure Mode:** **Interblocage** (Deadlock — violates Rule 2).
1. `T0` sets `etat[0] = true` and is **preempted**.
2. `T1` sets `etat[1] = true`.
3. `T0` spins on `while (etat[1])` (true) and `T1` spins on `while (etat[0])` (true). Neither ever yields, so **both are deadlocked forever**.

blocks.title: Attempt 5 / Tentative 5 (Slide 24): Set & Yield If Busy — Fails: Livelock / Starvation

annotations.note: Both threads back off when they see the other's flag, but without a tie-breaker they can loop in lockstep forever.

blocks.title: Attempt 5 Failure Trace & Summary Table
blocks.content:
**Failure Mode:** **Famine / Livelock** (Starvation — violates Liveness).
1. `T0` sets `etat[0] = true`; `T1` sets `etat[1] = true`.
2. Both enter their outer `while` loop (`etat[other]` is `true`).
3. Both back off simultaneously: `T0` sets `etat[0] = false` and `T1` sets `etat[1] = false`.
4. Both see `etat[other] == false`, exit the inner `while`, and re-set `etat[0] = true` and `etat[1] = true` in lockstep.
5. This symmetric dance can repeat **forever** without either thread ever entering the critical section.

| Attempt | Mechanism | Failure Mode (Slides 20–24) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | `while (occupe); occupe = true;` | **Pas d'exclusion** (Race between check and set) |
| **2** | `while (tour != i); ... tour = other;` | **Couplage** (Strict alternation blocks if other stops in non-CS) |
| **3** | `while (etat[other]); etat[i] = true;` | **Pas d'exclusion** (Race between check and set) |
| **4** | `etat[i] = true; while (etat[other]);` | **Interblocage** (Deadlock when both set `true`) |
| **5** | Set, then clear `etat[i] = false` inside `while (etat[other])` | **Famine** (Livelock in symmetric lockstep) |

sections.title: 3. Dekker's & Peterson's Algorithms + Multi-Core Barriers
sections.description: How Dekker and Peterson achieve software mutual exclusion, and why multi-core CPUs require memory fences.

blocks.title: Dekker's Algorithm: Conceptual Form & How the Backoff Loop Works (Slides 25–26)
Dekker's Algorithm: Complete Single-Core C++ (Slide 27)

annotations.note: Only the thread whose turn it is NOT backs off by clearing etat[0] = false.
On exit, pass turn to the other thread before clearing etat[0].

blocks.title: Why Multi-Core CPUs Break Dekker & Peterson (Slide 31)
blocks.content:
Mathematically, Dekker's and Peterson's algorithms are 100% correct. However, **modern multi-core processors** break them due to:
1. **Cache coherency delays** (*Cohérence des mémoires caches*): writes sit in a core's local store buffer before reaching shared cache/RAM.
2. **Out-of-order memory access reordering** (*Ordre des accès mémoires*): the CPU or compiler may execute a subsequent `load` (`while (etat[1])`) before an earlier `store` (`etat[0] = true`) is globally visible.

**Fix in C++:** Insert a memory synchronization barrier:
```cpp
#define BARRIER std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acq_rel)
```
This guarantees that **all `load` and `store` operations before the barrier complete and are visible before any `load` or `store` after the barrier**.

blocks.title: Dekker's Algorithm: Multi-Core C++ with Two BARRIERs (Slide 32)

annotations.note: BARRIER #1: Ensures etat[0] = true is globally visible before reading etat[1].
BARRIER #2: Ensures re-asserted etat[0] = true is globally visible before re-checking while (etat[1]).

blocks.title: Peterson's Algorithm: Single-Core C++ (Slide 30)

annotations.note: MUST come before tour = 1! Announce intention first.
Politely yield priority to the other thread (tour = 1).
Spin ONLY if the other thread wants in AND it is the other thread's turn.

blocks.title: Peterson's Algorithm: Multi-Core C++ with BARRIER (Slide 33)

annotations.note: Single BARRIER ensures both intention[0] = true and tour = 1 are visible before reading intention[1] and tour.

blocks.title: Critical Trap: Why `intention[0] = true` MUST Precede `tour = 1` + Dekker vs. Peterson
blocks.content:
> [!WARNING]
> **Order-of-Operations Trap:** What happens if you swap lines 6–7 in Peterson's algorithm (`tour = 1;` *before* `intention[0] = true;`)?
> 1. `T0` executes `tour = 1` and gets **preempted** before setting `intention[0] = true`.
> 2. `T1` runs `tour = 0; intention[1] = true;` (or `intention[1] = true; tour = 0;`).
> 3. `T1` checks `while (intention[0] && tour == 0)` $\rightarrow$ `intention[0]` is still `false`, so **`T1` enters the CS**.
> 4. `T0` resumes, sets `intention[0] = true`, and checks `while (intention[1] && tour == 1)` $\rightarrow$ `tour` is `0` (not `1`!), so **`T0` ALSO enters the CS**!
> **Mutual exclusion is broken!** Setting `intention[0] = true` *before* `tour = 1` ensures that if `T1` overwrites `tour = 0`, `T0`'s intention is already visible to `T1`.

### Dekker vs. Peterson Comparison

| Criterion | Dekker's Algorithm | Peterson's Algorithm |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Complexity** | Longer: nested `while` + `if (tour == other)` backoff | Concise: 2 assignments + 1 single `while` condition |
| **Who yields?** | Only the thread whose turn it is not clears `etat[i]` | Both politely set `tour = other`; the last writer waits |
| **Multi-core fences** | Requires **2** `BARRIER`s per task | Requires **1** `BARRIER` per task |
| **4 Rules + Fairness** | Satisfies all 4 rules + bounded wait | Satisfies all 4 rules + linear wait (at most 1 bypass) |

sections.title: 4. Active vs. Passive Waiting & Slide 35 Final Exercise
sections.description: Comparing busy-waiting to OS kernel primitives, plus the Slide 35 broken-protocol analysis.

blocks.title: Active Waiting vs. Passive Waiting (Slide 34)
blocks.content:
* **Active Waiting (*Attente active*):** Processor time is wasted testing a condition in a loop (`while (...) ;`) to block a process/thread (used by Dekker and Peterson).
* **Passive Waiting (*Attente passive*):** A waiting process/thread is **blocked by the OS kernel**, leaving the CPU available for other ready tasks. Requires kernel-supported primitives:
  * **Locks / Mutexes** (*Verrous*)
  * **Semaphores** (*Sémaphores*)
  * **Monitors** (*Moniteurs*)

> [!CAUTION]
> **Slide 34 Caveat:** Kernel primitives (*verrous, sémaphores, moniteurs*) make designing concurrent algorithms easier, **but they do NOT eliminate the risk of bugs!** Misplaced locks or wrong wait orders still cause deadlocks, race conditions, and starvation.

blocks.title: Slide 35 Exercise: Does This Protocol Guarantee Mutual Exclusion?

annotations.note: Danger! A preemption right before tour = 0 (or tour = 1) creates a fatal race window.

blocks.title: Analyze the Slide 35 Protocol
blocks.prompt:
**Question (Slide 35):** *L'exclusion mutuelle est-elle garantie par les parties prélude et postlude des tâches ? Justifiez votre réponse.*

Trace an execution starting from `tour = 0`, `intention = {false, false}` to prove whether mutual exclusion holds or fails.
self_check_criteria: Answered NO: mutual exclusion is NOT guaranteed.
Identified the exact preemption point: T1 exits `while (intention[0])` while `intention[0]` is still `false`, and is preempted right before `tour = 1`.
Showed that T0 then sees `tour == 0`, skips its `while (tour != 0)` loop completely, and enters the critical section.
Showed that T1 resumes, executes `tour = 1`, exits `while (tour != 1)`, and ALSO enters the critical section simultaneously.
blocks.model_answer:
**No, mutual exclusion is NOT guaranteed.**

**Counterexample (`tour = 0`, `intention = {false, false}`):**
1. `T1` sets `intention[1] = true`.
2. `T1` sees `tour != 1` (`tour == 0`), enters the outer `while`, and sees `intention[0] == false`, so it exits `while (intention[0])`.
3. **Context switch** right before `T1` executes `tour = 1`.
4. `T0` sets `intention[0] = true`, checks `while (tour != 0)` $\rightarrow$ `false` (since `tour` is still `0`), and **enters the critical section**.
5. `T1` resumes, sets `tour = 1`, re-evaluates `while (tour != 1)` $\rightarrow$ `false`, and **also enters the critical section**! Both tasks are now in the critical section simultaneously.

blocks.title: Slide 35 Counterexample: Both T0 and T1 Enter the Critical Section
blocks.caption: Because T1 checks intention[0] before setting tour = 1, a preemption right before tour = 1 lets T0 enter on the stale tour = 0.
blocks.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant T0 as "T0"
  participant S as "Shared (tour=0, int={F,F})"
  participant T1 as "T1"
  T1->>S: "1. intention[1] = true"
  T1->>S: "2. tour != 1 (0!=1) & intention[0] == false"
  Note over T1: Preempted right before tour = 1!
  T0->>S: "3. intention[0] = true"
  T0->>S: "4. Check tour != 0 -> FALSE (tour is 0)"
  Note over T0: T0 ENTERS CRITICAL SECTION!
  T1->>S: "5. Resumes: tour = 1"
  T1->>S: "6. Check tour != 1 -> FALSE (tour is 1)"
  Note over T1: T1 ALSO ENTERS CRITICAL SECTION!

sections.title: 5. Diagnostic Quiz & Spaced Repetition Flashcards
sections.description: Verify mastery of counter++ minimum = 2, Attempts 1–5, fairness types, Peterson's trap, and multi-core barriers.

blocks.question: Two threads each increment a shared `static int counter = 0;` `1,000,000` times without synchronization (`counter = counter + 1`). What is the theoretical minimum possible final value of `counter`?
blocks.explanation: T1 loads 0 and is preempted; T2 runs 999,999 iterations; T1 writes 1; T2 loads 1 on its final iteration and is preempted; T1 finishes its remaining 999,999 iterations; T2 writes 2.
hints: Consider what happens if T1 loads `counter = 0` into `r1` and is preempted before writing it back.
Can the same trick be repeated once more on T2's final iteration?

blocks.question: In **Attempt 5** (`etat[0] = true; while (etat[1]) { etat[0] = false; while (etat[1]); etat[0] = true; }`), what failure mode occurs?
options: Livelock / Starvation (Famine): both threads can infinitely set, clear, and re-set their flags in lockstep without entering the CS.
Deadlock (Interblocage): both threads spin forever with etat[0] == true and etat[1] == true.
Broken mutual exclusion: both threads enter the critical section simultaneously.
Strict coupling (Couplage): a thread stopped in its non-critical section blocks the other.
blocks.correct_answer: Livelock / Starvation (Famine): both threads can infinitely set, clear, and re-set their flags in lockstep without entering the CS.
blocks.explanation: Attempt 5 adds a backoff (`etat[i] = false`) to avoid Attempt 4's deadlock, but without a `tour` tie-breaker, both threads can back off and retry in lockstep forever (livelock/starvation).
hints: Notice that Attempt 5 clears `etat[0] = false` inside the loop, so it doesn't stay stuck in a static deadlock.
What happens if T0 and T1 execute the exact same instructions at the exact same pace?

blocks.question: According to Slide 16's waiting fairness taxonomy, what does **Linéaire** (*Linear*) waiting guarantee?
options: A task cannot access the resource twice while another task is waiting.
Tasks strictly enter the critical section in exact FIFO arrival order.
Waiting time is finite, though a task may be overtaken an unbounded number of times.
For n tasks, a waiting task can be overtaken by at most n! tasks.
blocks.correct_answer: A task cannot access the resource twice while another task is waiting.
blocks.explanation: Slide 16 defines Linear waiting as: 'une tâche ne peut accéder deux fois la ressource si une autre est en attente'. FIFO is strictly arrival-ordered; Finie is unbounded but finite.
hints: Compare FIFO, Linéaire, Bornée par f(n), and Finie from Slide 16.
Linear limits how many times a single competitor can re-enter ahead of a waiting task.

blocks.question: In Peterson's algorithm, what happens if `T0` swaps the order of its first two lines to `tour = 1;` followed by `intention[0] = true;` (and `T1` does the same)?
options: Mutual exclusion can be violated: both T0 and T1 can enter the critical section simultaneously.
Deadlock occurs immediately whenever both threads request the critical section.
It becomes identical to Dekker's algorithm.
It still works on single-core CPUs, only failing on multi-core CPUs.
blocks.correct_answer: Mutual exclusion can be violated: both T0 and T1 can enter the critical section simultaneously.
blocks.explanation: If T0 sets `tour = 1` and is preempted before `intention[0] = true`, T1 sees `intention[0] == false` and enters the CS (after setting `tour = 0`). When T0 resumes, `tour` is `0` (not `1`), so T0 also enters the CS.
hints: Trace what happens if T0 is preempted right after `tour = 1`.
What does T1 see when it checks `intention[0]`?

blocks.question: Why do Dekker's and Peterson's algorithms fail on modern multi-core CPUs unless `std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acq_rel)` (`BARRIER`) is added?
options: CPU cache coherency delays and out-of-order memory access reordering can allow both threads to read stale values and enter the critical section simultaneously.
C++ `bool` variables are not supported on multi-core processors.
Multi-core processors cannot execute `while` loops.
The `tour` variable overflows when two cores access it.
blocks.correct_answer: CPU cache coherency delays and out-of-order memory access reordering can allow both threads to read stale values and enter the critical section simultaneously.
blocks.explanation: Each core has its own store buffer and cache, and CPUs/compilers reorder independent loads and stores. `BARRIER` guarantees all prior loads/stores complete before subsequent loads/stores.
hints: What happens if Core 0 writes `intention[0] = true` to its local store buffer while reading `intention[1]` from cache?

blocks.question: In the multi-core C++ implementation of **Dekker's algorithm** (Slide 32), where must the **two** `BARRIER` calls be placed in `T0()`?
options: Right after the initial `etat[0] = true;` AND right after re-setting `etat[0] = true;` inside the `if (tour == 1)` backoff block.
Once at the start of `while (true)` and once inside the critical section.
Right before `etat[0] = true;` and right after `etat[0] = false;`.
Only once, right after `tour = 1;` at exit.
blocks.correct_answer: Right after the initial `etat[0] = true;` AND right after re-setting `etat[0] = true;` inside the `if (tour == 1)` backoff block.
blocks.explanation: Every time `T0` sets `etat[0] = true` and is about to test `while (etat[1])`, a `BARRIER` is required so the store to `etat[0]` is globally visible before the load of `etat[1]`.
hints: Look at every place where `etat[0] = true;` is followed by `while (etat[1])`.
How many times does `T0` set `etat[0] = true` in Slide 32?

blocks.title: The 4 Rules of Mutual Exclusion
blocks.front: What are the **4 rules** (Slide 17) that every valid mutual exclusion algorithm must satisfy?
blocks.back:
1. **Mutual Exclusion:** At most 1 task in the CS at any instant.
2. **No Deadlock:** If tasks wait and the CS is free, one enters in finite time.
3. **Independence (No Coupling):** Behavior outside the CS never blocks other tasks.
4. **Symmetry:** No task has a privileged role; identical algorithm for all.

blocks.title: Slide 16: 4 Waiting Fairness Types
blocks.front: Name and define the **4 waiting fairness types** from Slide 16.
blocks.back:
1. **FIFO:** Strict arrival order.
2. **Linéaire:** No task can enter twice while another is waiting.
3. **Bornée par $f(n)$:** For $n$ tasks, a waiting task is overtaken by at most $f(n)$ tasks.
4. **Finie:** Wait is unbounded by a function of $n$, but never infinite.
blocks.hint: FIFO -> Linéaire -> Bornée par f(n) -> Finie.

blocks.title: Attempts 1–5 Failure Modes
blocks.front: What is the exact failure mode of each of **Attempts 1–5** (Slides 20–24)?
blocks.back:
- **Attempt 1 (`occupe`):** No mutual exclusion
- **Attempt 2 (`tour`):** Coupling / strict alternation
- **Attempt 3 (`etat`, check then set):** No mutual exclusion
- **Attempt 4 (`etat`, set then check):** Deadlock (*interblocage*)
- **Attempt 5 (`etat`, set & yield):** Livelock / Starvation (*famine*)
blocks.hint: No excl -> Coupling -> No excl -> Deadlock -> Livelock.

blocks.title: Peterson's Algorithm & Order Trap
blocks.front: In Peterson's algorithm, what are the 3 lines of `T0`'s entry protocol, and why must `intention[0] = true` precede `tour = 1`?
blocks.hint: Announce intention BEFORE yielding the turn.

blocks.title: Active vs. Passive Waiting + Caveat
blocks.front: What is the difference between **active waiting** and **passive waiting**, and what caveat does Slide 34 emphasize?
blocks.back:
- **Active (*Attente active*):** Wastes CPU cycles spinning in a loop.
- **Passive (*Attente passive*):** OS kernel blocks the thread, freeing the CPU (via **locks/mutexes, semaphores, monitors**).
- **Caveat:** Kernel primitives simplify design, **but do NOT eliminate the risk of bugs** (deadlock, starvation, races).
blocks.hint: Busy loop vs. Kernel-blocked; primitives != bug-free.
